blocks.text: That the Hebrew name קורא kore does not signify the partridge, as has hitherto been believed, but a kind of woodcock (rusticula) or gallinago.

The bird called קורא kore in Hebrew is called קוראה koraa or קוריה korea in Chaldee, and قارية [qāriya] karia in Arabic. The sacred writers mention it in two places. [col. 81] In the first, David, a fugitive, addresses Saul thus, 1 Sam. XXVI, 20.: the king of Israel has come out to seek a single flea, כאשר ירדוף קורא בהרים, as if one were pursuing the bird kore in the mountains. The other passage reads thus, Ierem. XVII, 11.: The kore gathered, and did not bring forth: so he who amasses riches, but not by justice, will leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end will be a fool. From these passages we learn that the קורא kore is a mountain bird, not of great value, in the catching of which the fowler spends his effort badly; and that it is one of those birds which sit on the eggs of others. For this is what these words of Jeremiah mean, קורא דגר ולא ילד, the kore gathered, and did not bring forth, that is, it gathered the eggs of others, not laid by itself, to brood them under its shadow. Hence Es. XXXIV, 15., of the serpent קפוז kippoz, that is, the acontias or dart-snake, ודגרה בצלה, and it gathered in its shadow, that is, it brooded its eggs. And at Iob. XXXIX, 14., for תחמם, will warm, said of the ostrich's eggs, the Chaldee has תדגר, will gather. This needed to be pointed out, because many wrongly refer the verb to gather in Jeremiah to the ἐπισύναξιν [episynaxin] of the chicks. Among them are Hippolytus, Chrysostom, Olympiodorus, and among the Hebrews R. Selomo ^{(1)}. So much from Scripture.

[II, 633] In section 64 of the book Bereshit Rabba, which is both very ancient and of great authority among the Jews, a certain R. Joshua, son of Chanina, אסכולסטקיא דאורייתא, Scholastic of the Law, that is, a doctor of Theology, tells this fable about the same bird: ארי טרף טרף ועמד עצם בגרונו אמר כל דאתי מפיק ליה אנא יהיב ליה אגריה אתא הדין קורא מיצראה דמוקריה אריך יהיב מוקריה ואפקיה אמר ליה הב לי אגרי אמר ליה זיל תהא מלגלג ואומר דעלית לפומא דאריא בשלם ונפקית בשלם, A lion had devoured its prey, and a bone stuck in its throat, and it said: Whoever comes and draws it out, I will give him a reward. Then came an Egyptian kore with a long beak, which it put into the lion's throat and drew the bone out from there, and said, Give me my reward. But the lion answered, Go, and boast that you entered the lion's mouth in peace and came out in peace. This fable is the twin of this Aesopic one: Λύκου λαιμῷ ὀστέον ἐπεπήγει. ὁ δὲ γεράνῳ μισθὸν παρέξειν εἶπεν, εἰ, τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτῆς ἐπιβαλοῦσα, τὸ ὀστοῦν ἐκ τοῦ λαιμοῦ αὐτοῦ ἐκβάλοι. ἡ δὲ τοῦτ᾽ ἐκβαλοῦσα, δολιχόδειρος οὖσα, τὸν μισθὸν ἐπεζήτει. ὅστις γελάσας, καὶ τοὺς ὀδόντας θήξας, Ἀρκεῖ σοι μισθὸς, ἔφη. τοῦτο καὶ μόνον, ὅτι καὶ λύκου στόματος καὶ ὀδόντων ἐξῆρες κάραν σῶαν, μηδὲν παθοῦσαν. [Lykou laimō osteon epepēgei. ho de geranō misthon parexein eipen, ei, tēn kephalēn autēs epibalousa, to ostoun ek tou laimou autou ekbaloi. hē de tout᾽ ekbalousa, dolichodeiros ousa, ton misthon epezētei. hostis gelasas, kai tous odontas thēxas, Arkei soi misthos, ephē. touto kai monon, hoti kai lykou stomatos kai odontōn exēres karan sōan, mēden pathousan.] That is, in the rendering of Phaedrus, book 1, Fable 8:

When a bone he had swallowed stuck in a wolf's throat, overcome by great pain he began to entice each one with a reward to draw out that evil. At last a crane was persuaded by his oath, and, trusting the length of her neck to his gullet, performed a dangerous cure on the wolf. When she demanded a reward for this deed, "You are ungrateful," he said, "you who have carried your head away unharmed from our mouth, and you ask for payment."

Yet there is no reason for anyone to conclude, from comparing the Hebrew fable with the Greek and Roman, that the bird קורא kore is the same as the crane. For just as the Hebrews substituted the lion for the wolf, [II, 634] so they could substitute another bird for the crane. But at least we gather this: that the bird kore has a long beak. All the Hebrews assert the same. The Aruch, under קר, fifth entry: עוף הוא ופיו שמנקר בו ארוך ביותר, It is a bird whose mouth, that is, beak, is very long. So also R. Aquinas and David de Pomis: קורא צפור שיש לו מקרא ארוך, Kore, a bird having a long beak.
